title: Midterm muddle, the Google search fiasco, & your AI teacher is glitching
author: Alexander Russo
summary: This weekly issue of The Grade is a curated digest of education journalism, with Alexander Russo's commentary on the week's big story and short reviews of three standout pieces. The lead argues that the Democratic midterm wins cannot be attributed to education, that school funding referenda had mixed results, and that Democratic control does not guarantee better outcomes for kids. The featured journalism covers a Bloomberg investigation into online provider Stride and Texas funding for students who do not attend, a Boston Globe series on absenteeism, and Chalkbeat's account of a failed public Christian school in Colorado. Russo's own column asks who will be the Pablo Torre of K-12 coverage, urging shoe-leather reporting, transparency and video. The rest is a roundup of people, numbers, events and quotes from the education media world.
points: Education was one issue among many in the midterms, and Democratic wins should not be read as a clear mandate on schools.
Public funding rules that pay virtual schools like brick-and-mortar ones can steer money to providers with poor attendance and outcomes.
Massachusetts coverage quantifies post-2020 absenteeism at roughly 15 million additional missed school days.
Russo argues education reporters can learn from successful podcasters: old-fashioned reporting, vulnerability, varied formats and video.
Sal Khan's shift from predicting AI would transform education to saying its net effect is negative is flagged as the week's sharpest reversal.
quotes: The big education story of the week is the big blue wave for Democrats in the midterms — combined with the mixed outcomes for schools and vulnerable students. Tuesday’s midterms resulted in big wins for Democratic candidates for office — many of whom have pledged support for public schools and opposition to private school choice and other red-coded approaches

Despite the understandable urge, few if any Democratic wins — including Talarico and Hinojosa — can definitively be attributed to education, given voters’ focus on inflation, Iran, AI/data centers, immigration, and government corruption

Last but not least, Democrats in office often mean greater financial support for public school systems but they do not necessarily mean better results for kids. Students have often languished under Democratic control. Several of the states making the most progress in recent years have been controlled by Republicans.
The Lone Star State mandates that virtual schools receive the same funding per-pupil as any other public school — despite fewer expenses and an abysmal record of student attendance and outcomes.
The takeaway number: the increased absenteeism rate post 2020 has led to 15 million more missed days of school.
The formula for success includes old-fashioned shoe-leather reporting, deep vulnerability and transparency, a variety of formats, and video.

Seventy-five percent of kids in the US will soon go to school under a Democratic governor . Almost 2/3ds of states are now signed up for the federal education tax credit, with New Mexico becoming the 32nd . The US comes in last for teacher pay across more than 30 industrialized countries.
